questiontext.text:
Here is another conjecture: for all {@condB@}, {@eqB@}.

Disprove it by giving a counterexample. Type fractions as 1/2 and \(\sqrt{2}\) as sqrt(2).

\(a=\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] \(b=\) [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]

generalfeedback.text:
To disprove a for all statement, choose values that satisfy its conditions and show that the two sides differ for those values.

Here the conjecture is about {@condB@}. Take \(a={@ceA@}\) and \(b={@ceB@}\), which satisfy these conditions. Then the left-hand side of {@eqB@} is {@ceLv@} and the right-hand side is {@ceRv@}. These are different, so the conjecture is false.

The conjecture is true for some values, for example \(a={@holdA@}\), \(b={@holdB@}\), where both sides equal {@hLv@}. That is why trying one or two values is not enough to decide whether a conjecture is true. (For {@condShortB@}, the two sides are equal exactly when {@whenB@}.)

{@ruleB@}

questionnote.text: Variant {@vB@}: {@wordsB@}. Sample counterexample a = {@ceA@}, b = {@ceB@}; trap pair a = {@holdA@}, b = {@holdB@}.

falsefeedback.text: Your values are not ones the conjecture talks about: it is only about {@condB@}. A counterexample has to satisfy the conditions of the conjecture.

node.description: Diagnostic: values at which the conjecture holds

truefeedback.text: With \(a={@sa@}\) and \(b={@sb@}\) the left-hand side is {@Lv@} and the right-hand side is {@Rv@}. They are different, so the conjecture is false.

falsefeedback.text: With \(a={@sa@}\) and \(b={@sb@}\) both sides are equal ({@Lv@} and {@Rv@}), so the conjecture is true for these values. This is not a counterexample: a false conjecture can still be true for some values. Try other values.
